papers.title: MultiCardioFusionNet: A multimodal fusion model for predicting coronary heart disease integrating time-domain, frequency-domain, and clinical information.
papers.abstract: Coronary heart disease (CHD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, highlighting the need for accurate, accessible, and cost-effective diagnostic approaches. This study proposes MultiCardioFusionNet, a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates electrocardiographic (ECG) signals and clinical information (gender, age, and body mass index) for intelligent CHD diagnosis. To capture complementary disease-related characteristics, a three-branch architecture is designed to jointly extract Frequency-Domain features, temporal features, and clinical representations from multimodal data. The resulting multimodal representations are integrated through an attention-guided fusion strategy to exploit complementary information across spectral, temporal, and clinical domains. The framework was developed and evaluated using real-world multicenter clinical data. In the internal validation cohort, MultiCardioFusionNet achieved an AUC of 0.9327, while independent external validation yielded an AUC of 0.9261, demonstrating promising generalizability capability. The proposed model consistently outperformed several representative deep learning methods, including Gated Recurrent Unit, Convolutional Neural Network, Convolutional Neural Network - Long Short-Term Memory, Convolutional Neural Network - Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory and Convolutional Neural Network - Transformer (GRU, CNN, CNN-LSTM, CNN-BILSTM, and CNN-transformer). These results indicate that integrating electrophysiological and clinical information can substantially enhance CHD diagnosis. The consistent performance across the internal test cohort and the independent multi-center external validation cohort suggests that MultiCardioFusionNet may serve as a non-invasive decision-support approach for assisting CHD identification and risk assessment among clinically suspected patients undergoing further diagnostic evaluation.

papers.title: A Dual Soft Attention Network for Automatic Sleep Staging via Single-Lead Electrocardiogram Signals.
papers.abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) is the current gold standard for sleep monitoring; however, it is complex, burdensome, and costly. In contrast, commercial health monitoring devices, such as the Apple Watch, offer sleep scoring at a low cost over a few days. This paper proposes a dual-attention mechanism-based sleep staging method using single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, named SleepECGNet. The method extracts multi-scale features by employing convolutional kernels of different sizes, thereby capturing subtle details in the ECG signals. The model then integrates an SE module and a Luong attention-based encoder-decoder architecture to filter redundant information and dynamically focus on different sleep stages. Experiments were conducted using the HMC, MGH, and SHHS1 datasets for sleep staging tasks and the Apnea-ECG corpus was employed to execute transfer learning strategies directed at sleep apnea recognition. Comprehensive ablation experiments were conducted to verify the effectiveness of each component. Moreover, an analysis of sequence duration demonstrated that expanding the input timeframe directly improves classification outcomes.

papers.title: Machine learning and evolutionary computation for increased reliability of wearable devices for monitoring cardiac arrhythmias in the wild.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
papers.abstract: Continuous analysis of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is essential for diagnosing cardiovascular diseases, particularly arrhythmias, which contribute significantly to global mortality. With the increasing use of wearable devices for non-clinical cardiac monitoring, real-time ECG processing encounters challenges due to memory constraints, particularly when memory is wasted by recording false positives. Noise in real-life ECG monitoring, such as motion artifacts, complicates automatic arrhythmia detection and recording, and calls for efficient methods to selectively filter out noisy signals that may be falsely classified (and recorded) as arrhythmias in devices with limited storage. This study develops and systematically compares machine learning and deep learning approaches for ECG noise detection using real-world wearable data acquired outside controlled clinical environments. By employing various models for classification, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Multi-Layer Perceptron, Gradient Boosting and Convolutional Neural Networks, we investigated four approaches, using as input features: i) raw signal data, ii) Heart Rate Variability-related time-domain features, iii) a combination of Heart Rate Variability-related time-domain and frequency-domain features, and iv) the parameters of a Genetic Programming-based reconstruction algorithm, analyzing both memory and computational requirements and classification performance of the corresponding architectures. Our findings indicate that the Multilayer Perceptron model, combined with Heart Rate Variability-related time- and frequency-domain features, offers an optimal trade-off between accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score. This study presents a scalable classification approach specifically designed for real-life arrhythmia detection in wearable devices, demonstrating the potential to enhance continuous cardiac monitoring and to facilitate the integration of such algorithms into wearable devices suitable for clinical and real-world settings.

papers.title: Language-supervised electrocardiogram interpretation with vision transformer.
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Most artificial intelligence models for electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation rely on task-specific supervised learning, requiring dedicated labeled datasets for each diagnostic task and limiting scalability across diverse cardiac conditions. This study investigated whether vision-language learning from paired ECG recordings and summary reports could enable transferable ECG representations without task-specific supervised training.

METHODS: We developed ECG-VLM, a contrastive vision-language model consisting of a Transformer-based image encoder and a text encoder, trained on 800,034 paired 10-s ECG recordings and summary reports from the MIMIC-IV-ECG database. Cardiac condition detection was performed using natural-language prompts without condition-specific retraining or fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated on an internal test set and externally validated using the LSAS-ECG dataset (45,151 recordings) across 14 cardiac conditions, together with retrieval and subgroup analysis.

RESULTS: ECG-VLM achieved diagnostic performance across 14 cardiac conditions, with AUROC ranging from 0.679 to 0.981 on the internal test set and from 0.691 to 0.991 on external validation. Performance was strongest for rhythm abnormalities (mean AUROC 0.948 internally and 0.921 externally) and lower for morphological conditions. Compared with the previously reported signal-based ECG-CLIP framework, ECG-VLM achieved comparable performance for rhythm abnormalities while improving AUPRC for several morphological conditions. Performance remained broadly consistent across external validation and demographic and clinical subgroups.

CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of vision-language supervision from paired ECG recordings and summary reports for learning transferable ECG representations without task-specific supervised training. This framework provides a basis for future extension of vision-language learning to ECG images encountered in routine clinical practice.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13755-026-00482-7.

papers.title: Memristor-based echo state network for ECG classification: optimizing accuracy and efficiency with different architectures.
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signal classification is a crucial task in automated cardiac monitoring and early disease detection. Conventional machine learning and deep learning methods often face challenges related to high computational costs, large data requirements and difficulty in handling real-time ECG analysis. In this work, we have proposed three memristor-based echo state network (MESN) models for ECG classification: (1) MESN, (2) Parallel MESNs (PMESN) with a classifier and (3) Attention-enhanced MESN (AMESN), where all three models employ artificial neural network (ANN) as a readout layer. These models leverage the property of an ESN to transform ECG signals into high-dimensional representations, thereby enhancing classification performance. The proposed models were evaluated on different benchmark ECG datasets: ECG200, ECG5000, ECGFiveDays, NonInvasiveFetalECGThorax1, NonInvasiveFetalECGThorax2, and TwoLeadECG. The results demonstrate that AMESN achieves the highest precision, recall, F1-score and overall accuracy particularly excelling in datasets with high intra-class variability. Whereas, PMESN improves robustness by leveraging multiple reservoir layers, while MESN provides a strong baseline with computational efficiency. These models are also compared with other state-of-the-art models and the analysis shows that AMESN achieves 1.92-13.39% higher accuracy, demonstrating superior performance. These findings highlight the potential of ESN as a lightweight yet powerful approach for ECG classification, making it suitable for integration into wearable and IoT-based healthcare systems.

papers.title: KDM-Net: a large-kernel and Bi-Mamba integrated network for 12-lead atrial arrhythmia classification.
papers.abstract: Objective.Automatic recognition of atrial arrhythmias is important for early clinical screening and computer-aided diagnosis. Distinguishing atrial fibrillation from atrial flutter remains challenging because of their similar electrocardiographic manifestations and high risk of misclassification. This study aimed to develop an effective model for atrial arrhythmia classification with improved multi-lead feature utilization, long-range temporal modeling, and cross-patient generalization.Approach.We propose KDM-Net, which takes 12-lead electrocardiogram signals as input. The network employs a large-kernel K module to enhance the perception of waveform morphology and rhythm patterns, a D module to recalibrate and fuse multi-lead features, and a bidirectional Mamba-based M module to model long-range temporal dependencies. KDM-Net was evaluated on the combined CUSPH and PTB-XL dataset under an inter-patient protocol.Main results.In five-fold cross-validation, KDM-Net achieved an average accuracy and1-score of 96.04% and 89.21%, respectively. On the independent patient-level test set, the accuracy and1-score were 96.41% and 88.31%, respectively. On the CinC 2020 external test set, the model achieved an accuracy and1-score of 91.14% and 80.41%, respectively. KDM-Net outperformed several representative models in comparative experiments.Significance.KDM-Net effectively integrates multi-lead spatial information and long-range temporal dependencies, demonstrating strong recognition performance and promising cross-patient generalization. It provides an effective solution for the intelligent diagnosis of atrial arrhythmias.

papers.title: MKP-ECG: A Knowledge-Enhanced Dual-Stream Network for Robust Arrhythmia Classification with Medical Prior-Guided Multi-Loss Optimization.
papers.abstract: Accurate classification of cardiac arrhythmias from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is essential for clinical decision-making, yet deep learning models often struggle with minority classes such as Fusion beats (F-type) owing to severe class imbalance and insufficient integration of domain knowledge. In this work, we propose Medical Knowledge Prior Network (MKP-ECG), a knowledge-enhanced dual-stream network for four-class arrhythmia classification (N, S, V, F) following the AAMI standard. The first stream employs a multi-scale CNN with residual connections and squeeze-and-excitation attention to learn data-driven representations from raw waveforms. The second stream, termed the Medical Prior Module, extracts a 34-dimensional clinical feature vector encoding morphology, rhythm, template matching, and rule-based indicators that mirror the reasoning process of cardiologists. The two streams are fused through explicit feature concatenation and a knowledge attention gate that dynamically modulates neural representations based on clinical evidence, and are jointly optimized by a composite loss function comprising two novel medical knowledge prior losses: a knowledge graph KL-divergence loss that aligns predictions with expert-defined electrophysiological priors and a clinical constraint loss that penalizes predictions contradicting established diagnostic criteria. Evaluated on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database under the inter-patient DS1/DS2 paradigm with methodologically corrected data augmentation (waveform-only SMOTE with nearest-neighbor clinical feature copying and purity-weighted contrastive loss), MKP-ECG achieves 99.14% accuracy, 92.77% Macro-F1, and 76.98% F-class F1-score with perfect F-recall, representing a 51.7% relative improvement over the knowledge-free baseline. Independent evaluation on the INCART database, where the model is trained and tested entirely within INCART using the same architecture and hyperparameters without any dataset-specific tuning, provides encouraging evidence of architectural generalizability under a record-split protocol, achieving 99.71% accuracy and 87.43% F-class F1-score.

papers.title: Electrocardiogram-Based Deep Learning to Prioritize Testing for Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy.
papers.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is a treatable cause of heart failure, but diagnosis is often delayed. Accessible tools to prioritize confirmatory evaluation could reduce missed diagnoses when cardiac imaging is limited.

OBJECTIVE: To develop and validate a locally deployable artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled system that identifies patients for further ATTR-CM evaluation from routine electrocardiography (ECG) images.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This diagnostic test study used an AI-ECG model developed within Yale New Haven Health (using ECGs from August 2015-June 2023) and temporally validated (July 2023-July 2025). External validation included 5 multinational cohorts and 3 screening cohorts (older Black and Hispanic adults with heart failure; adults with prior carpal tunnel surgery; 99-3902 individuals per cohort).

EXPOSURE: Use of AI-ECG for detecting ATTR-CM from routine ECG images or raw 12-lead signals.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values for ATTR-CM confirmed by cardiac amyloid radionuclide imaging (CARI) or biopsy. An exploratory analysis evaluated sequential screening with AI-ECG followed by AI-enabled echocardiography.

RESULTS: Development used 28 174 ECGs from 11 291 patients (293 with ATTR-CM). In internal validation (44 123 patients; mean age, 68.5 years; 49.7% female), AUROC was 0.84 (95% CI, 0.79-0.89), with sensitivity of 0.72 and specificity of 0.86 at the prespecified threshold, and was maintained in a specificity stress test among patients with features that mimic ATTR-CM (left ventricular hypertrophy or severe aortic stenosis without amyloid; AUROC, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.75-0.86]) and those referred for CARI (AUROC, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.73-0.84]). Across 5 external cohorts, AUROCs ranged from 0.78 to 0.89. In 3 screening cohorts, AUROCs were 0.76 (95% CI, 0.68-0.83) in the SCAN-MP study (n = 645) and 0.79 (95% CI, 0.65-0.93) and 0.91 (95% CI, 0.82-0.97) in 2 CACTUS study cohorts (n = 251, n = 121). Sequential AI-ECG and AI-enabled echocardiography increased the positive predictive value from 0.24 to 0.66 and reduced sensitivity from 0.84 to 0.68.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Locally deployable AI applied to ECG images discriminated ATTR-CM across multinational retrospective and screening cohorts. This approach may provide an accessible first step to prioritize selected patients for echocardiography and confirmatory imaging, although intended use and calibration require prospective evaluation.
authors: Robert M A van der Boon

papers.title: Scaling to Multimodal and Multichannel Heart Sound Classification with Synthetic and Augmented Biosignals.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for approximately 17.9 million deaths each year. Effective treatment requires early detection, which can be achieved with accurate and inexpensive pre-screening. This study uses a wearable vest which records real-world phonocardiogram (PCG) data from several auscultation sites at once (mPCG), but the cohort is small and the recordings noisy. To improve classification performance despite this limited, noisy dataset, signal processing augmentation and the denoising diffusion models WaveGrad and DiffWave supply additional training data for fine-tuning a pre-trained Wav2Vec 2.0 encoder. This work evaluates augmentation across three settings with increasingly complex inputs and smaller recording datasets: single-channel PCG, synchronised PCG and electrocardiogram (ECG), and six-channel mPCG. Accuracy, unweighted average recall (UAR) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) reach 92.98%, 92.48% and 0.8064 on the Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2016 single-channel PCG dataset, 93.14%, 92.21% and 0.8380 on its synchronised PCG-ECG training-a subset, and 77.13%, 74.25% and 0.5082 on the vest mPCG dataset. On a separate 40-subject vest hold-out, the SVM achieves mean accuracy, UAR and MCC of 79.17%, 72.22% and 0.574, respectively. Ablations examine pre-training, augmentation, generated data and encoder adaptation. For the primary classification configurations, the combination of original, conventionally augmented and generated data gives the highest mean performance.

papers.title: MRAST-Net: A Lightweight Multi-Receptive-Field Residual Temporal Network for 12-Lead ECG Classification.
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals play an important role in cardiovascular disease screening, clinical monitoring, and remote healthcare. However, existing high-performing ECG classification methods usually rely on complex deep learning architectures, which often involve a large number of parameters, high computational cost, and limited deployability in resource-constrained scenarios. To balance classification performance and lightweight deployment, this paper proposes MRAST-Net, a lightweight multi-receptive-field residual temporal network for 12-lead ECG classification. The proposed model first employs a lead mixing layer to enable cross-lead information interaction. It then uses a lightweight multi-scale residual depthwise convolution module to extract local waveform morphology features under different receptive fields, while an efficient channel attention mechanism is introduced to enhance informative channel responses. On this basis, a temporal convolutional network is further incorporated to model long-range dynamic dependencies, and attentive statistics pooling is used to aggregate global statistical features for final multi-label classification. Experiments on two public 12-lead ECG datasets, PTB-XL and CPSC-2018, show that the proposed model achieves AUC scores of 93.12 $\pm$ 0.16\%, 92.29 $\pm$ 0.80\%, and 92.62 $\pm$ 0.51\%, and ACC scores of 89.17 $\pm$ 0.09\%, 96.40 $\pm$ 0.02\%, and 97.72 $\pm$ 0.07\% on the 5-superclass, 23-subclass, and 44-diagnostic-class tasks of PTB-XL, respectively. On CPSC-2018, MRAST-Net achieves an AUC of 96.57 $\pm$ 0.43\% and an ACC of 96.59 $\pm$ 0.26\% under 5$\times$3 nested cross-validation. These results demonstrate that MRAST-Net achieves competitive classification performance while maintaining a low parameter scale, indicating its potential for deployment in resource-constrained scenarios such as portable monitoring devices, real-time assisted diagnosis, and primary healthcare.

papers.title: Multimodal deep learning approach for frailty classification using electrocardiogram and chest X-ray imaging.
papers.abstract: Frailty is a critical age-related syndrome associated with increased risks of disability, hospitalization, and mortality. While Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) is the standard for evaluation, it is often subjective, time-consuming, and resource-intensive. To address these limitations, this study developed and validated a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates chest X-rays (CXR) and electrocardiograms (ECG) to provide an objective and rapid tool for frailty classification. We retrospectively analyzed data from 2,830 older adults who underwent CGA between 2007 and 2024, partitioned chronologically into training, validation, and test sets. Frailty was defined using a Multidimensional Frailty Score (MFS) > 5. Three deep learning models were trained and evaluated: a CXR-only model (EVA-X vision transformer), an ECG-only model (DenseNet-121), and a multimodal model combining both inputs. The multimodal model outperformed the single-modality models and four non-imaging clinical baseline models incorporating age, sex, comorbidity index, or routine laboratory variables, achieving the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.778 and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.726. For continuous MFS estimation, the multimodal model achieved the highest Pearson correlation (r = 0.610) and the lowest mean absolute error (MAE = 1.68) among the evaluated models. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was used to qualitatively explore the image regions that influenced model predictions. This multimodal AI framework demonstrates modest classification performance and feasibility for frailty screening. By leveraging routinely collected clinical images, this framework may serve as a practical screening adjunct to identify older adults who may benefit from formal CGA. Further studies are needed to determine its clinical utility when applied preoperatively for the stratification of postoperative risk.

papers.title: Multiscale temporal deep learning for ECG waveform estimation from contactless radar signals.
papers.abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is widely used for monitoring cardiac activity and supporting the assessment of cardiovascular conditions. Conventional ECG systems require skin-contact electrodes, which may cause discomfort and limit their suitability for prolonged monitoring. Contactless radar sensing provides a non-contact approach for capturing chest-wall movements associated with cardiac activity. However, ECG waveform estimation from radar signals is challenging because radar measures mechanical chest-wall motion, whereas ECG represents electrical cardiac activity. In addition, respiratory interference, motion artifacts, phase distortion, and inter-subject variability can affect the relationship between radar and ECG signals. This study presents a multiscale temporal deep learning framework for ECG waveform estimation from contactless radar signals. The proposed framework combines radar signal preprocessing, feature extraction, multiscale residual convolutional learning, bidirectional long short-term memory networks, and multi-head attention to learn temporal and local signal representations from radar-derived features. Radar in-phase and quadrature () signals are processed through phase extraction, denoising, and feature extraction to construct the input representation for ECG estimation. The framework was evaluated using a publicly available synchronized radar-ECG dataset containing 30 subjects under the resting scenario. A subject-independent evaluation protocol was used, with separate participants assigned to training, validation, and testing subsets. Across five repeated subject-independent randomized splits, the proposed framework achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.07584, a root mean square error of 0.14261 and Pearson correlation coefficient (Pearson) of 0.64459. These results demonstrate the feasibility of estimating the overall temporal structure of ECG waveforms from contactless radar measurements under resting conditions.

papers.title: Subject-independent framework for protocol-defined stress task classification using multimodal physiological signals.
papers.abstract: Prolonged stress can cause cardiovascular disease, depression, and anxiety. Reliable detection is therefore important. Existing studies using multimodal physiological methods have already reported accuracy, up to 99.7% however, two important aspects remain underexplored. First, most studies separate stress only from a neutral baseline, amusement, and different workload levels. Second, subject-independent performance remains limited because most studies evaluate their models using subject-dependent data splits that are prone to data leakage. This proposed study tries to address these gaps. Protocol-defined stress tasks are detected from everyday activities, not from any workload levels. The proposed model, a one-dimensional convolutional neural network, is evaluated subject-independently using leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation. This proposed study was conducted on the GalaxyPPG dataset. The dataset includes ECG, PPG, and BVP signals. This enables multimodal fusion for stress detection during everyday activities. Single modalities achieve mean test accuracies of 62.19% for PPG, 67.74% for BVP, and 47.81% for ECG on LOSO. Fusion (ECG+PPG+BVP) achieves the mean test accuracy on LOSO evaluation,. To the best of the author's knowledge, this modality's combination (ECG+PPG+BVP) has not been explored in the literature for Galaxy PPG dataset.

papers.title: An adaptive multi-scale dilated convolutional neural network for arrhythmia detection.
papers.journal: Computer methods in biomechanics and biomedical engineering
papers.abstract: The rising global incidence of arrhythmia calls for reliable detection methods. Most existing approaches suffer from poor generalization and insufficient feature extraction for long-term electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. This work proposes an adaptive multi-scale dilated convolutional network (AMSDNet). It uses multi-scale dilated convolutions, gated adaptive weight allocation, and spatial attention fusion to capture global ECG features. Validated on Massachusetts Institute of Technology-Beth Israel Hospital Arrhythmia Database (MIT-BIH), the China Physiological Signal Challenge (CPSC) 2018, and the Computing in Cardiology Challenge (CINC) 2017 datasets, our method outperforms state-of-the-art models with average accuracy of 99.7%, 91.8% and 83.7%, respectively.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Cardiovascular Disease: Current Applications, Methodological Challenges, and Clinical Translation.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), is increasingly being investigated for cardiovascular diagnosis, risk stratification, and prognostic assessment, leveraging electrocardiography, cardiovascular imaging, electronic health records, wearable devices, and molecular data. This review summarizes current AI applications in ischemic heart disease, acute coronary syndromes, heart failure, arrhythmias, and structural cardiovascular disease, and critically examines the methodological requirements for clinical translation. Particular attention is given to model taxonomy, data leakage, overfitting, external validation, calibration, dataset shift, explainability, clinical utility, privacy, cybersecurity, and regulatory considerations. Current evidence shows that AI can identify clinically relevant patterns and may complement conventional cardiovascular assessment; however, high performance in retrospective or selected datasets does not necessarily translate into improved patient outcomes. Therefore, robust patient-level data separation, independent external and prospective validation, calibration assessment, workflow evaluation, and post-deployment monitoring are essential. Emerging multimodal, hybrid, and foundation-model approaches may further improve cardiovascular prediction, but their clinical value requires rigorous evaluation. Currently, AI should primarily be regarded as a complementary decision-support tool rather than a replacement for established diagnostic or prognostic standards.
